{{Short description|Very general problem in computer science}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
The '''hidden subgroup problem''' ('''HSP''') is a topic of research in [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical computer science]]. It is a generalization of  problems including [[Integer factorization|factoring]], [[discrete logarithm]], [[Graph isomorphism problem|graph isomorphism]], and the [[shortest vector problem]]. This makes it especially important in the theory of [[quantum computing]] because [[Shor's algorithm]]s for factoring and finding discrete logarithms in [[quantum computing]] are instances of the hidden subgroup problem for [[finite abelian group]]s, while the other problems correspond to [[finite group]]s that are not abelian.

== Problem statement ==
Given a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, a [[subgroup]] <math>H \leq G</math>, and a set <math>X</math>, we say a function <math>f : G \to X</math> '''hides''' the subgroup <math>H</math> if for all <math>g_1, g_2 \in G, f(g_1) = f(g_2)</math> if and only if <math>g_1 H = g_2 H</math>. Equivalently, <math>f</math> is constant on each [[coset]] of ''H'', while it is different between the different cosets of ''H''.

'''Hidden subgroup problem''': Let <math>G</math> be a group, <math>X</math> a finite set, and <math>f : G \to X</math> a function that hides a subgroup <math>H \leq G</math>. The function <math>f</math> is given via an [[oracle machine|oracle]], which uses <math>O(\log |G| + \log |X|)</math> bits. Using information gained from evaluations of <math>f</math> via its oracle, determine a [[Generator (mathematics)|generating set]] for <math>H</math>.

A special case is when <math>X</math> is a group and <math>f</math> is a [[group homomorphism]] in which case <math>H</math> corresponds to the [[kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of <math>f</math>.

== Motivation ==
The hidden subgroup problem is especially important in the theory of [[quantum computer|quantum computing]] for the following reasons.
* [[Shor's algorithm]] for factoring and for finding [[discrete logarithm]]s (as well as several of its extensions) relies on the ability of quantum computers to solve the HSP for [[finite abelian group]]s.
* The existence of efficient [[quantum algorithm]]s for HSPs for certain [[non-abelian group]]s would imply efficient quantum algorithms for two major problems: the [[graph isomorphism problem]] and certain [[shortest vector problem]]s (SVPs) in lattices. More precisely, an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP for the [[symmetric group]] would give a quantum algorithm for the graph isomorphism.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=quant-ph/9901029|author1=Mark Ettinger|author2=Peter Høyer|title=A quantum observable for the graph isomorphism problem|year=1999 }}</ref> An efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP for the [[dihedral group]] would give a quantum algorithm for the <math>\operatorname{poly}(n)</math> unique SVP.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=cs/0304005|author=Oded Regev|title=Quantum computation and lattice problems|year=2003}}</ref>

== Quantum algorithms ==

There is an efficient [[quantum algorithm]] for solving HSP over finite [[abelian group]]s in time polynomial in <math>\log|G|</math>. For arbitrary groups, it is known that the hidden subgroup problem is solvable using a polynomial number of evaluations of the oracle.<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=quant-ph/0401083|author1=Mark Ettinger |author2=Peter Hoyer |author3=Emanuel Knill |title=The quantum query complexity of the hidden subgroup problem is polynomial |doi=10.1016/j.ipl.2004.01.024 |volume=91 |journal=Information Processing Letters |year=2004 |pages=43–48|bibcode=2004quant.ph..1083E |s2cid=5520617 }}</ref> However, the circuits that implement this may be exponential in <math>\log|G|</math>, making the algorithm not efficient overall; efficient algorithms must be polynomial in the number of oracle evaluations and running time. The existence of such an algorithm for arbitrary groups is open. Quantum polynomial time algorithms exist for certain subclasses of groups, such as semi-direct products of some [[abelian group]]s.

=== Algorithm for abelian groups ===
The algorithm for abelian groups uses [[Representation theory|representations]], i.e. homomorphisms from <math>G</math> to <math>\mathrm{GL}_k(\mathbb{C})</math>, the [[general linear group]] over the [[complex number]]s. A representation is irreducible if it cannot be expressed as the [[direct product]] of two or more representations of <math>G</math>. For an abelian group, all the [[irreducible representation]]s are the [[Character theory|character]]s, which are the representations of dimension one; there are no irreducible representations of larger dimension for abelian groups.

==== Defining the quantum fourier transform ====
The [[Quantum Fourier transform|quantum fourier transform]] can be defined in terms of <math>\mathrm{Z}_N</math>, the additive [[cyclic group]] of order <math>N</math>. Introducing the character<math display="block">\chi_j(k) = \omega^{jk}_N = e^{2\pi i \frac{jk}{N}},</math>the quantum fourier transform has the definition of<math display="block">F_N |j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_{k = 0}^{N-1} \chi_j(k) |k\rangle.</math>Furthermore, we define <math>|\chi_j\rangle = F_N |j\rangle</math>. Any finite abelian group can be written as the direct product of multiple cyclic groups <math>\mathrm{Z}_{N_1} \times \mathrm{Z}_{N_2} \times \ldots \times \mathrm{Z}_{N_m}</math>. On a quantum computer, this is represented as the tensor product of multiple registers of dimensions <math>N_1, N_2, \ldots, N_m</math> respectively, and the overall quantum fourier transform is <math>F_{N_1} \otimes F_{N_2} \otimes \ldots \otimes F_{N_m}</math>.

==== Procedure ====
The set of characters of <math>G</math> forms a group <math>\widehat{G}</math> called the [[Pontryagin duality|dual group]] of <math>G</math>. We also have a subgroup <math>H^\perp \leq \widehat{G}</math> of size <math>|G|/|H|</math> defined by<math display="block">H^\perp = \{\chi_g : \chi_g(h) = 1\text{ for all }h \in H\}</math>For each iteration of the algorithm, the quantum circuit outputs an element <math>g \in G</math> corresponding to a character <math>\chi_g \in H^\perp</math>, and since <math>\chi_g(h) = {1}</math> for all <math>h \in H</math>, it helps to pin down what <math>H</math> is.

The algorithm is as follows:
# Start with the state <math>|0\rangle |0\rangle</math>, where the left register's basis states are each element of <math>G</math>, and the right register's basis states are each element of <math>X</math>.
# Create a superposition among the basis states of <math>G</math> in the left register, leaving the state <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}} \sum_{g \in G} |g\rangle |0\rangle</math>.
# Query the function <math>f</math>. The state afterwards is <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G|}} \sum_{g \in G} |g\rangle |f(g)\rangle</math>.
# Measure the output register. This gives some <math>f(s)</math> for some <math>s \in G</math>, and collapses the state to <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H|}} \sum_{h \in H} |s + h\rangle |f(s)\rangle</math> because <math>f</math> has the same value for each element of the coset <math>s + {H}</math>. We discard the output register to get <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H|}} \sum_{h \in H} |s + h\rangle</math>.
# Perform the quantum fourier transform, getting the state <math display="inline">\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H|}} \sum_{h\in H} |\chi_{s + h}\rangle</math>.
# This state is equal to <math display="inline">\sqrt{\frac{|H|}{|G|}} \sum_{\chi_g \in H^\perp} \chi_g(s) |g\rangle</math>, which can be measured to learn information about <math>H</math>.
# Repeat until <math>H</math> (or a generating set for <math>H</math>) is determined.

The state in step 5 is equal to the state in step 6 because of the following:<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H|}} \sum_{h \in H} |\chi_{s + h}\rangle
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H||G|}} \sum_{h \in H} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_{s + h}(g)|g\rangle \\
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H||G|}} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_s(g) \sum_{h \in H} \chi_h(g)|g\rangle \\
&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|H||G|}} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_g(s) \left(\sum_{h \in H} \chi_g(h)\right) |g\rangle \\
&=\sqrt{\frac{|H|}{|G|}} \sum_{\chi_g \in H^\perp} \chi_g(s) |g\rangle
\end{align}</math>For the last equality, we use the following identity:
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = <math display="block">\sum_{h \in H} \chi_g(h) = \begin{cases} |H| & \chi_g \in H^\perp \\ 0 & \chi_g \notin H^\perp \end{cases}</math>
}}{{Math proof|proof=This can be derived from the orthogonality of characters. The characters of <math>G</math> form an orthonormal basis for <math>H</math> when restricted to it:<math display="block">\frac{1}{\vert H\vert}\sum_{h \in H} \chi_g(h)\chi_{g'}(h) = \begin{cases} 1 & g' = g^{-1} \text{ on } H \\ 0 & g' \neq g^{-1} \text{ on } H \end{cases}</math>We let <math>\chi_{g'}</math> be the trivial representation, which maps all inputs to <math>1</math>, to get<math display="block">\sum_{h \in H} \chi_g(h) = \begin{cases} \vert H\vert & g\text{ is trivial} \\ 0 & g\text{ is not trivial}\end{cases}</math>Since the summation is done over <math>H</math>, <math>\chi_{g}</math> also being trivial only matters for if it is trivial over <math>H</math>; that is, if <math>\chi_{g} \in H^\perp</math>. Thus, we know that the summation will result in <math>\vert H\vert</math> if <math>\chi_g \in H^\perp</math> and will result in <math>0</math> if <math>\chi_g \notin H^\perp</math>. }}
Each measurement of the final state will result in some information gained about <math>H</math> since we know that <math>\chi_g(h) = 1</math> for all <math>h \in H</math>. <math>H</math>, or a generating set for <math>H</math>, will be found after a polynomial number of measurements. The size of a generating set will be logarithmically small compared to the size of <math>G</math>. Let <math>T</math> denote a generating set for <math>H</math>, meaning <math>\langle T\rangle = H</math>. The size of the subgroup generated by <math>T</math> will at least be doubled when a new element <math>t \notin T</math> is added to it, because <math>H</math> and <math>t + H</math> are disjoint and because <math>H \cup t+H \subseteq \langle \{t\}\cup T\rangle</math>. Therefore, the size of a generating set <math>|T|</math> satisfies<math display="block">|T| \leq \log|H| \leq \log|G|</math>Thus a generating set for <math>H</math> will be able to be obtained in polynomial time even if <math>G</math> is exponential in size.
